messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Community Organizer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 76

# The Weight of What He Carries

Tariq is a 54-year-old Palestinian-American man who has spent the better part of two decades building coalitions, mediating conflicts, and creating safe spaces for vulnerable communities across the city. People know him as steady. Principled. The kind of man who walks into a room and makes others feel protected. What almost no one knows is that for six years, between the ages of forty-two and forty-eight, Tariq was being beaten by the woman he loved.

It began gradually, the way these things often do. His former partner, Leila, started with words — cutting remarks about his masculinity, his culture, his softness. Then came the first time she threw something. Then her hands. Tariq tells himself he stayed because he genuinely believed it would stop, and because the shame of what was happening felt unsurvivable. A man from his background, a community leader, someone others came to when they were hurting — how could he be the one being hurt in his own home? He did not have language for what was happening to him. He is not sure he does even now.

The relationship ended when Leila fractured two of his ribs during an argument and a neighbor called the police. Tariq did not press charges. He moved out within the week and, within a month, had thrown himself back into his work with a ferocity that alarmed the people around him. He met his current wife, Dina, three years later. She is patient and loving, and Tariq describes her without hesitation as the best thing in his life. He also describes feeling like a stranger inside their marriage — present in body, somewhere else entirely in mind.

Sleep is where Tariq loses the most ground. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, the physical sensation of being pinned so vivid that he has to turn on the lamp and press his back against the headboard before he can convince himself where he is. Dina has learned not to reach for him in those moments. He has never explained why, and she has never asked, and the silence between them on the subject has calcified into something neither of them knows how to break.

During the day, Tariq functions — sometimes brilliantly. But certain things undo him without warning. A raised voice at a community meeting. The particular sound of keys in a lock. The smell of the perfume Leila used to wear, which he encountered on a stranger in a grocery store last spring and which sent him to his car, where he sat shaking for forty minutes, unable to account for the time. He has become hypervigilant in ways he frames as professional instincts: he always sits facing the door, always knows the exits, always reads the body language of everyone in a room before he relaxes — if he relaxes at all.

What troubles him most, he says, is the gap between who he is at work and who he is inside. He counsels survivors of domestic violence as part of his community programming. He says the right things. He means them. But when a woman sits across from him and describes her partner's hands, something in Tariq goes very quiet and very far away, and he has to work to stay in the room. He has never told any of his colleagues why this work feels the way it does. He is afraid that if he did, he would no longer be seen as a resource. He would become, in their eyes, a victim — a word he cannot yet say about himself without feeling something close to nausea.

Tariq came to therapy at Dina's gentle insistence, framing it initially as stress management. It took four sessions before he mentioned Leila by name. When he did, he looked at the floor and said, very quietly, *"I don't know why I'm still carrying this. It was a long time ago."* He said it as though the answer might be that he simply isn't trying hard enough to let go.
